text.description: Article body. Concatenated with `title` to form the `content` field the models are trained on.

subject.description: Publisher-assigned topic category. Metadata only - never used as a feature, because it leaks the label.

date.description: Publication date. Stored as free text in several formats ('December 31, 2017', '31-Dec-17'), so it is parsed leniently rather than typed.

checks.name: Source files fingerprinted
checks.summary: 2 source files hashed (SHA-256) and recorded.
checks.remedy: Quote these hashes next to any reported accuracy figure.

checks.name: Data unchanged since last run
checks.summary: All source files byte-identical to the previous run.
checks.remedy: If the data changed, retrain and re-evaluate; cached models are stale.

checks.name: Column set and dtypes match EXPECTED_SCHEMA
checks.summary: Both files carry exactly the four expected columns (title, text, subject, date), all object/string dtype.
checks.remedy: Update EXPECTED_SCHEMA deliberately, or fix the extract.

checks.name: Label is implicit in the filename
checks.summary: Neither CSV contains a label column; the label comes from which file a row was read from. Any row that moves between files silently changes class, and there is no way to detect that from the data.
checks.remedy: Materialise an explicit `label` column (and a source_file column) when the two CSVs are merged, so provenance survives the join.

checks.name: No missing or blank required fields
checks.summary: 631 blank cells across 44,898 rows. Worst column: `text` in Fake.csv at 2.68% (630 rows).
checks.remedy: Rows with an empty `text` still carry a title, so `content` is non-empty and they survive load_data(). Decide explicitly whether a headline-only row is a valid training example - currently it is treated as one.

checks.name: No exact duplicate articles
checks.summary: 5,795 of 44,898 rows (12.9%) are exact duplicates of an earlier row. 0 article texts appear under both labels.
checks.remedy: load_data(drop_duplicates=True) removes these, and it must run BEFORE train_test_split - otherwise the same article lands on both sides of the split and test accuracy is inflated.

checks.name: Headlines are distinct
checks.summary: 6,169 repeated headlines (13.7%). After exact-body deduplication 374 repeated headlines remain, i.e. different bodies published under the same headline.
checks.remedy: Same-headline/different-body pairs are usually a story and its update; they are near-duplicates for training purposes.

checks.name: No near-duplicate articles
checks.summary: Exhaustive, whole corpus: normalising case, punctuation and whitespace turns 272 further rows (0.6%) into duplicates that `drop_duplicates("content")` leaves in place. Sampled, MinHash+LSH over 6,000 of the 39,103 unique articles: 12 pairs at estimated Jaccard >= 0.80, touching 24 articles (0.4% of the sample), of which 10 are the punctuation-only kind and 0 straddle the fake/real boundary. That sample covers only 2.4% of all possible pairs, so the sampled rate is a lower bound, not an estimate - the exhaustive number above is the one to act on.
checks.remedy: Exact deduplication is not enough: near-duplicates split across the train/test boundary leak just as effectively. Deduplicate on a hash of the normalised text - that is O(n), needs no threshold, and catches the punctuation-only pairs for free. Raise --near-dup-sample to search harder for the genuinely fuzzy ones.

checks.name: Articles do not share identical openings
checks.summary: 6,116 rows repeat an earlier row's first 120 normalised characters. 5,795 of those are exact duplicates already counted above, leaving 321 rows (0.7%) that open identically but are not identical texts.
checks.remedy: Cheap linear screen: one hash per row, no pairwise comparison. Run it before the MinHash join to see whether the expensive step is even needed.

checks.name: Dates parse and fall in the declared range
checks.summary: 10 of 44,898 date values (0.022%) do not parse; 9 of those contain a URL instead of a date. 0 parsed dates fall outside 2015-01-01..2018-12-31.
checks.remedy: These rows are scraper failures - the URL landed in both `title` and `date`. Drop them; they carry no article text worth training on.

checks.name: Headlines are headlines, not URLs
checks.summary: 9 rows have a URL in the `title` field.
checks.remedy: Same scraper failure as the unparseable dates - the two overlap.

checks.name: Text decodes cleanly as UTF-8
checks.summary: No U+FFFD replacement characters, no mojibake sequences and no C0 control characters (0 total). 19 cells contain zero-width or bidi format characters, and 25,575 contain non-ASCII characters - almost all of them curly quotes, which clean_text() strips anyway.
checks.remedy: Normalise Unicode (NFKC) and strip format characters at load time if the vectorizer is ever changed to keep punctuation.

checks.name: Article length is plausible
checks.summary: 610 articles (1.4%) are under 20 words, 12 are over 6,000. 631 rows have an empty body and consist of the headline alone. Median 385 words, max 8,389.
checks.remedy: A headline-only row teaches the model headline style, not article content. Either drop them or record that the effective corpus is mixed.

checks.name: Articles are not all-caps or mostly punctuation
checks.summary: 82 articles are more than 60% uppercase characters and 3 are less than 50% letters. Both skew heavily fake (82 and 1 respectively), so they are a style signal as much as a defect.
checks.remedy: Do not silently delete these - they are real examples of the fake style. Flag them so the effect on the model can be measured.

checks.name: Subject categories are shared across classes
checks.summary: 8 of 8 subject values appear in exactly one class. Predicting the majority class of an article's `subject` scores 100.00% accuracy on the whole corpus, with no text and no model involved.
checks.remedy: `subject` must never be used as a feature, and its presence means the two files came from different scrapes rather than one sampling frame. Treat it as evidence about provenance, not as metadata.

checks.name: Publication dates overlap across classes
checks.summary: Fake articles span 2015-03-31..2018-02-19, real articles 2016-01-13..2017-12-31. 2,926 articles (6.5%) fall outside the shared window, and 100.0% of them are fake - the date alone classifies them.
checks.remedy: Restrict both classes to the shared window before drawing any conclusion about model skill, or accept that part of the accuracy is calendar arithmetic.

checks.name: No single token identifies a class
checks.summary: The literal string `(Reuters)` appears in 99.2% of real articles and 0.0% of fake ones. "Contains it, therefore real" scores 99.60% on the whole corpus with no model. The two classes are not fake vs real news; they are one wire service vs a set of blogs.
checks.remedy: Every accuracy figure from this dataset must be quoted next to this number. `python src/train.py --strip-boilerplate` retrains without the marker; the drop is the leakage share. See `reports/eda_report.md` for the full marker sweep.

checks.name: Classes are reasonably balanced
checks.summary: fake 23,481 / real 21,417; minority class is 47.7% of the corpus. No resampling needed.

checks.name: Article length distributions agree
checks.summary: KS statistic 0.110 (p=3.65e-118), Jensen-Shannon distance 0.298 on the length histogram. Median 390 words fake vs 377 real - a 13-word difference. A KS statistic of 0.11 is a small effect: length is the dimension on which these two files come closest to agreeing, and it is also the only one a scraper does not control.
checks.remedy: With n>17,000 per class the KS p-value is effectively zero for any difference at all, so read the statistic (effect size), not the p-value.

checks.name: Vocabulary distributions agree
checks.summary: Jensen-Shannon distance 0.397 between the two unigram distributions on a 8,000-article sample; term-set Jaccard overlap 0.849 over the 20,000 terms that survive min_df=3. (`src/eda.py` reports Jaccard 0.34 for the same corpus - that figure includes the long tail of once-seen tokens, which is where the two files diverge most. Neither number is wrong; they measure different vocabularies.) Some vocabulary difference is expected between real and fabricated news; the question is whether it is topical or publisher-specific, and the leakage audit in `src/eda.py` says largely the latter.
checks.remedy: Re-run this after `strip_source_boilerplate()` to see how much of the gap is Reuters datelines rather than content.

checks.name: Publication date distributions agree
checks.summary: Jensen-Shannon distance 0.482 on the monthly publication histogram - which on its own looks unremarkable, because both classes are dense through the middle of the period. The decisive number is that 11 of 35 months (31%) contain articles from one class only. A single divergence statistic hides a hard calendar boundary; this check reports both and takes the worse verdict.
checks.remedy: Sample both classes from the same calendar window, or state plainly that the model has a date confound it cannot separate.
